title: Why tokens cost money
description: Every token in and out of a language model is metered: input tokens, output tokens, at per-million rates that differ by model. A 100k-token context window used carelessly costs dollars per request; shaped carefully, cents. Token efficiency is not frugality for its own sake — it is latency (fewer tokens = faster), quality (signal over noise), and cost, all at once.
mechanism: Cost = (input_tokens x input_rate + output_tokens x output_rate). Measure per feature; budget per request; alert on drift. The cheapest token is the one never sent.
algo: Arithmetic, but measured per feature — the breakdown drives the shaping.
demo:
# the bill: tokens in + tokens out, per million
IN_RATE, OUT_RATE = 3.00, 15.00  # $ per 1M tokens (example tier)

def cost(in_tok, out_tok):
    return in_tok / 1e6 * IN_RATE + out_tok / 1e6 * OUT_RATE

sloppy = cost(100_000, 2_000)   # whole docs dumped into context
shaped = cost(8_000, 2_000)     # retrieved chunks + tight prompt
print('sloppy prompt: $%.2f per request' % sloppy)
print('shaped prompt: $%.2f per request' % shaped)
print('at 10k requests/day: $%.0f vs $%.0f per day' % (sloppy * 10000, shaped * 10000))

title: Prompt compression
description: Prompt compression shrinks inputs while keeping meaning: drop filler words, compress verbose JSON to compact forms, replace repeated boilerplate with references. LLMLingua-style compressors learn which tokens the model attends to and prune the rest — 5-10x compression with minimal quality loss on many tasks. The rule is task-dependent: compression that is safe for classification can break precise reasoning.
mechanism: Budget-based pruning (keep the highest-attention tokens), structural compression (tables -> CSV, JSON -> minimal), and demonstration compression (fewer, better few-shot examples). Validate on the task's eval set — never compress blind.
algo: O(tokens) compression; quality validated per task on evals.
demo:
# structural compression: verbose JSON -> compact form, same facts
import json

verbose = {
    'user': {'first_name': 'Ada', 'last_name': 'Lovelace', 'age': 36},
    'request': {'action': 'summarize', 'target': 'document_42'},
}
compact = 'user=Ada Lovelace,36; action=summarize; target=document_42'
v, c = len(json.dumps(verbose)), len(compact)
print('verbose: %d chars' % v)
print('compact: %d chars (%.1fx smaller, same facts)' % (c, v / c))
print('compress structure first (free), learned pruning second (validate!)')

title: Context pruning
description: Retrieved context is mostly noise: pruning keeps the chunks that matter for this query and drops the rest. Techniques: relevance re-ranking then top-k cutoff, duplicate removal (near-dup chunks waste tokens saying the same thing), and query-focused extraction (keep the sentences that answer, not the whole page). Pruning is where RAG quality comes from — retrieval finds candidates, pruning picks the evidence.
mechanism: Retrieve k=50 -> re-rank -> keep top 8 -> dedup by similarity -> extract relevant spans. Token budget per query caps the total. Log what was pruned for debugging.
algo: O(k log k) re-rank; dedup O(k^2) on the small set. Budget-bounded.
demo:
# retrieve 50 -> re-rank -> dedup -> keep 3: the pruning funnel
chunks = [('doc%d' % i, 0.9 - i * 0.02, 'content %d' % i) for i in range(10)]
chunks[5] = ('doc5', 0.65, 'content 1')  # near-duplicate of doc1

ranked = sorted(chunks, key=lambda c: -c[1])[:5]
seen, kept = set(), []
for doc, score, content in ranked:
    if content in seen:
        continue  # dedup: same content, wasted tokens
    seen.add(content)
    kept.append((doc, score))
    if len(kept) == 3:
        break
print('retrieved 10 -> pruned to:', kept)
print('re-rank, dedup, budget: retrieval finds, pruning picks the evidence')

title: Structured prompts
description: Structured prompts (XML tags, markdown sections, JSON schemas) beat prose walls: the model parses sections reliably, follows the schema, and the output validates. <context>, <instructions>, <examples>, <task> — the structure is a contract both sides understand. It also compresses: a schema says in 10 tokens what prose takes 100 to hedge.
mechanism: Sections with clear delimiters; schemas for inputs and outputs; examples in the same structure. Validate outputs against the schema; retry with the error on mismatch.
algo: O(1) structure overhead; output validation is schema-check cheap.
demo:
prompt = '''<context>
User is on the Pro plan; last login 2 days ago.
</context>
<task>
Summarize the ticket in one sentence.
</task>
<output>
{"summary": "..."}
</output>'''
print(prompt)
print()
print('sections > prose walls: parseable, validatable, and shorter')
print('output schema enforced: retry with the schema error on mismatch')

title: Few-shot selection
description: Few-shot examples teach by showing, but each example costs tokens — so choose few and well. Selection strategies: diversity (cover the input space), similarity (nearest neighbors of the query), and difficulty (include the tricky cases). Three great examples beat ten mediocre ones; the eval set decides which three. Dynamic selection (per-query neighbors) beats a fixed set on varied tasks.
mechanism: Example bank with embeddings; per query, retrieve the k most similar + 1-2 diverse; order by relevance. Evaluate example sets on the task eval — keep the winners.
algo: O(bank) retrieval per query (ANN for large banks). Quality from selection, not count.
demo:
# dynamic few-shot: nearest-neighbor examples per query, not a fixed set
bank = [
    ('translate "hello"', 'hola'),
    ('translate "goodbye"', 'adios'),
    ('summarize: ...', '...'),
    ('translate "thanks"', 'gracias'),
]

def select(query, k=2):
    qw = set(query.split())
    scored = sorted(bank, key=lambda e: -len(qw & set(e[0].split())))
    return scored[:k]

print('query: translate "please"')
for ex, out in select('translate "please"'):
    print('  example: %-22s -> %s' % (ex, out))
print('per-query neighbors beat a fixed set on varied tasks')

title: Token budgets
description: Token budgets cap each request's spend: max input tokens, max output tokens, per feature, per user, per day. The budget shapes design — features that cannot fit the budget must retrieve smarter, not spend more. Enforcement is at the gateway (count before send, truncate or reject over budget), and the budget dashboard shows who spends what. Budgets turn token efficiency from advice into architecture.
mechanism: Gateway counts tokens per request (fast tokenizer); enforces per-feature/per-user caps; over-budget requests get truncated context (least-relevant first) or rejected with a clear error. Dashboards per feature/user/day.
algo: O(tokens) counting; enforcement O(1) per request.

title: Prompt caching
description: Prompt caching reuses the model's computed state for repeated prefixes: the system prompt + context cached once, then each request only processes the new suffix. Anthropic's prompt caching cuts cost 90% and latency 85% for repeated-prefix workloads (agentic loops, long documents). The requirement is prefix stability — put the stable content first, the varying query last.
mechanism: Mark cacheable prefix (system + stable context); provider caches its KV state; requests with the same prefix hit the cache. Design prompts prefix-stable: instructions and docs first, user query last.
algo: O(1) cache hit on the prefix; only the suffix is computed. Savings proportional to prefix length.
demo:
# prefix-stable design: stable content first (cached), varying query last
STABLE = '<system>...5000 tokens of instructions...</system><docs>...20000 tokens...</docs>'

def request_cost(query_tokens, cache_hit):
    stable, q = 25000, query_tokens
    if cache_hit:
        return (stable * 0.1 + q)  # cached prefix at 10% price
    return stable + q

print('no cache : %d tokens billed' % request_cost(500, False))
print('cached   : %d tokens billed (prefix-stable design)' % request_cost(500, True))
print('rule: stable first, varying last -- the cache key is the prefix')

title: Batching requests
description: Batching amortizes the per-request overhead: ten classification tasks in one prompt cost one round trip and share the instructions prefix. The batch prompt lists items, demands indexed outputs, and parses them back apart. Limits: output length caps, error isolation (one bad item should not poison the batch), and latency (batching waits to fill). Async batch APIs (OpenAI's) give 50% discounts for non-urgent work.
mechanism: Accumulate items up to N or T ms; one prompt with numbered items; parse indexed outputs; map back. Per-item validation; failures retried individually.
algo: O(batch) items per call; cost per item drops toward the marginal token cost.
demo:
# one prompt, ten items, indexed outputs parsed back apart
items = ['great product', 'terrible service', 'ok i guess', 'love it!']

prompt = 'Classify each as POS/NEG/NEU. Reply as numbered lines.\n'
for i, it in enumerate(items):
    prompt += '%d. %s\n' % (i + 1, it)
print(prompt)
# 'model output' (simulated):
out = '1. POS\n2. NEG\n3. NEU\n4. POS'
results = {}
for line in out.splitlines():
    n, label = line.split('. ')
    results[items[int(n) - 1]] = label
print('parsed back:', results)
print('one round trip, shared instructions: batch when latency allows')

title: Distillation for prompts
description: Distillation moves work from prompt to weights: fine-tune a small model on (long prompt -> good output) pairs, and the small model learns the behavior without the long prompt. The 10k-token instruction set becomes baked-in behavior; runtime prompts shrink to the task. It trades upfront training cost for permanent per-request savings — the math favors it past thousands of requests per day.
mechanism: Collect (prompt, output) pairs from the big model; fine-tune the small model; verify quality on evals; deploy with short prompts. Re-distill as the big prompt evolves.
algo: O(training) upfront; O(1) per request after. Break-even at thousands of requests/day.
demo:
# break-even: when does distilling the long prompt pay off?
long_prompt_tokens = 10000
short_prompt_tokens = 200
price_per_1k = 0.003
train_cost = 50.0  # fine-tune cost

per_req_saving = (long_prompt_tokens - short_prompt_tokens) / 1000 * price_per_1k
reqs_per_day = 5000
payback_days = train_cost / (per_req_saving * reqs_per_day)
print('saving per request: $%.4f' % per_req_saving)
print('training cost $%.0f pays back in %.1f days at %d req/day' % (train_cost, payback_days, reqs_per_day))
print('past the break-even: permanent per-request savings')

title: Prompt templates
description: Prompt templates parameterize the stable parts: one template, many requests, with slots for the variables. They standardize quality (every request gets the good instructions), enable versioning (template v3 vs v4 in experiments), and make token budgets predictable (template tokens are constant). The template registry is versioned like code — because it is code.
mechanism: Templates with {slots}; versioned registry; render per request; A/B test versions on evals. Linters check templates for token bloat and missing sections.
algo: O(1) render. Versioning + evals make improvement systematic.

title: Evaluation of prompts
description: Prompt changes need evals: a fixed set of (input, expected) pairs scored automatically, run on every template change. Without evals, prompt edits are vibes — 'it feels better'. The eval set covers the task's dimensions (easy, hard, adversarial); the metric is task success, not token count. Token efficiency is a constraint on the eval-passing prompts, not the goal itself.
mechanism: Eval set per task; automatic scoring where possible (exact match, LLM judge for open-ended); run in CI on template changes; block regressions. Track tokens-per-passing-eval as the efficiency metric.
algo: O(eval set) per change. The eval set is the asset — curate it like tests.

title: Cost modeling
description: Cost modeling predicts the AI bill before it arrives: per-feature token histograms x rates, projected to traffic. The model has three inputs — measured tokens per request (p50/p99), request volume, and the rate card — and it answers 'what if we switch models?' or 'what if traffic 10x?'. Surprises come from the long tail: p99 token counts, not means, drive the bill.
mechanism: Histogram tokens per feature; multiply by volume and rates; scenario-model (model switch, traffic growth, optimization). Alert when actuals diverge from the model.
algo: Arithmetic on measured histograms. p99, not mean, drives cost.
demo:
# the bill is driven by p99 tokens, not the mean
import random
random.seed(2)
# token counts: mostly small, long tail of huge contexts
toks = [random.randint(500, 2000) for _ in range(950)] + [random.randint(50000, 100000) for _ in range(50)]
mean = sum(toks) / len(toks)
sorted_t = sorted(toks)
p99 = sorted_t[int(0.99 * len(toks))]
RATE = 3.0 / 1e6
vol = 100000
print('mean tokens: %d -> predicted bill $%.0f' % (mean, mean * RATE * vol))
print('p99  tokens: %d -> actual bill    $%.0f' % (p99, mean * RATE * vol))
print('same bill math -- but capacity and budget need the TAIL, not the mean')

title: Latency vs tokens
description: Latency scales with tokens: time-to-first-token depends on input length (prefill), and each output token takes time (decode). Halving the prompt roughly halves prefill latency; streaming hides decode latency. The latency budget therefore is a token budget in disguise — and the same shaping that saves money saves milliseconds. Measure prefill vs decode separately; they optimize differently.
mechanism: Prefill O(input) parallel; decode O(1) per token serial. Stream outputs; cap output tokens per feature; shape inputs for prefill. SLOs per feature, not global.
algo: Prefill parallel, decode serial — the fundamental asymmetry.

title: Quality guardrails
description: Efficiency must not silently degrade quality: guardrails assert output quality per request — schema validation, self-consistency checks, and sampled human review. When compression or pruning goes too far, the guardrail catches it (validation failure, low confidence) and the system falls back to the uncompressed prompt. Efficiency is a dial; guardrails are the stops.
mechanism: Validate every output (schema); score confidence; sample for human review; fallback to full context on failure. Track quality metrics alongside token metrics — both on the dashboard.
algo: O(1) validation per request; sampling O(1) amortized. Fallback bounded by the retry budget.

title: Tooling for token efficiency
description: The token-efficiency stack: tokenizers for counting (tiktoken), gateways for budgets and caching (LiteLLM), eval harnesses for quality, and dashboards for spend. Count before you send (never trust estimates), cache what repeats, evaluate what changes. The tooling makes efficiency a property of the pipeline, not a virtue of the individual prompt author.
mechanism: Count with the real tokenizer; enforce at the gateway; evaluate in CI; dashboard per feature. Same loop as performance engineering: measure, change, verify.
algo: O(tokens) counting with the real tokenizer — estimates lie, counts don't.

print('1. count   : real tokenizer (tiktoken), before every send')
print('2. enforce : gateway budgets + prompt caching (LiteLLM)')
print('3. evaluate: CI evals on every template change')
print('4. observe : per-feature dashboards (tokens, $, quality)')
print()
print('estimates lie, counts don\'t: measure > estimate, always')
